title: Chest Drainage System Position: Keep It Upright and Below the Chest
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A chest drainage unit should remain upright and below chest level so air/fluid can leave the pleural space without flowing back toward the patient.
recognize: System above chest, tipped unit, dependent loops, kinks, or compressed tubing can impair drainage.
priorities: Restore safe system position and tubing alignment, then reassess respiratory status.
assessMonitor: Check system position, tubing, insertion site, breath sounds, oxygenation, dyspnea, drainage trend.
interventions: Secure tubing and device according to manufacturer/facility policy; avoid routine clamping.
medicationSafety: Analgesia may support deep breathing/mobility but does not correct drainage malfunction.
redFlags: Sudden loss of drainage with distress
teaching: Do not lift the drainage unit onto the bed or above the chest during mobility.
delegationScope: Position checks may be shared; abnormal findings and respiratory changes require licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Placing the collection unit on the bed for convenience.
oneLinePearl: Chest drain stays upright, patent, and below the chest.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube drainage system safety principles

title: Chest-Tube Air Leak: Continuous Bubbling Needs a Source Check
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Unexpected continuous bubbling in a water-seal chamber can indicate an air leak from the patient, tubing, connections, or device. Reassess the patient first, then troubleshoot per policy without prolonged clamping.
recognize: New bubbling, audible leak, loose connection, worsening subcutaneous emphysema, dyspnea.
priorities: Assess respiratory status and system integrity; notify RN/provider if leak persists or patient worsens.
assessMonitor: Air-leak indicator, oxygenation, breath sounds, tube connections, dressing, subcutaneous emphysema.
interventions: Secure loose connections and follow facility/manufacturer troubleshooting steps.
medicationSafety: No medication corrects a mechanical air leak.
teaching: Report new bubbling/noise or sudden shortness of breath.
delegationScope: Troubleshooting that involves clamping or system manipulation is policy/competency dependent.
examTrap: Clamping the chest tube and leaving it clamped while looking for the leak.
oneLinePearl: Patient first, then system—never prolonged clamp troubleshooting.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube troubleshooting principles

title: Chest-Tube Drainage Change: Trend Matters More Than One Number
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A sudden surge of bright-red drainage or an abrupt stop in expected drainage can signal bleeding, obstruction, dislodgement, or a change in the underlying condition.
recognize: Rapidly increasing sanguineous drainage, abrupt zero drainage, new pain/swelling, dyspnea.
priorities: Assess patient, tubing patency, insertion site, and trend; escalate concerning changes promptly.
assessMonitor: Amount/color/character of drainage, vital signs, oxygenation, chest findings, tubing kinks.
interventions: Mark/time drainage levels and maintain unobstructed tubing; do not strip routinely.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use may increase bleeding risk and should be communicated when drainage changes.
teaching: Explain that abrupt output changes need immediate review.
delegationScope: Output measurement may be delegated; interpretation/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming no drainage always means improvement.
oneLinePearl: Sudden more or sudden none can both be dangerous.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube monitoring principles

title: Chest-Tube Dislodgement: Cover, Call, Reassess
bottomLine: A chest tube pulled out of the patient is an emergency. Protect the insertion site with the facility-approved occlusive dressing approach, call for help, and watch closely for tension physiology.
recognize: Tube out of chest, sudden open tract, dyspnea, subcutaneous emphysema, falling oxygenation.
priorities: Stay with patient, call emergency/provider support, cover site per protocol, reassess ABCs.
assessMonitor: Respiratory effort, oxygenation, breath sounds, tracheal position, hemodynamics.
interventions: Prepare for possible reinsertion and emergency imaging/intervention.
medicationSafety: Analgesia does not delay emergency respiratory management.
teaching: Secure tubing during mobility to reduce accidental traction.
delegationScope: Emergency response must follow facility policy and licensed scope.
examTrap: Trying to push the chest tube back into the insertion tract.
oneLinePearl: Tube out of chest = cover, call, assess—never reinsert blindly.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube dislodgement guidance

title: Tension Pneumothorax With a Chest Tube: Think Kink, Clamp, Blockage, Dislodgement
bottomLine: A patient with a chest tube can still develop tension physiology if the tube or vent is obstructed, clamped, kinked, or displaced. Acute distress requires immediate emergency escalation.
recognize: Sudden severe dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds, hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation, obstructed tubing.
priorities: Call emergency help and rapidly inspect for obvious external obstruction while supporting ABCs.
assessMonitor: Respiratory status, chest symmetry, oxygenation, hemodynamics, tubing/system.
interventions: Correct external kinks/clamps if within role/policy and prepare for emergency decompression by qualified clinician.
medicationSafety: Do not delay emergency decompression for routine medication administration.
teaching: Patients should avoid compressing or pulling tubing.
examTrap: Increasing wall suction without checking for a kinked or clamped tube.
oneLinePearl: Chest tube present does not rule out tension pneumothorax.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube complication principles

title: Transport With a Chest Tube: Preserve Drainage Without Routine Clamping
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: During transport, keep the drainage unit upright and below chest level and preserve the ordered water-seal/suction plan. Routine clamping for transport can create dangerous pressure buildup.
recognize: Tubing pulled taut, unit lifted above chest, accidental clamp, disconnected suction.
priorities: Verify transport plan, tubing security, emergency supplies, and patient stability before movement.
assessMonitor: Respiratory status before/during/after transport, tube connections, device position.
interventions: Disconnect wall suction only as ordered/appropriate; maintain water seal/device function per manufacturer instructions.
medicationSafety: Coordinate analgesia before movement when ordered to support ventilation and mobility.
teaching: Patient should move carefully and avoid grabbing tubing.
delegationScope: Transport assistance may be delegated; chest-drain assessment remains licensed responsibility.
examTrap: Clamping the chest tube before transport just to prevent spills.
oneLinePearl: Transport safely by preserving flow—not by routine clamping.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube transport principles

title: Subcutaneous Emphysema: New or Spreading Crepitus Needs Review
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New or rapidly spreading crepitus around a chest tube can signal an air leak, tube malposition, or inadequate drainage and should be escalated.
recognize: Crackling under skin, swelling around chest/neck, new dyspnea, increasing air leak.
priorities: Assess breathing and system integrity, mark/track spread if policy allows, notify RN/provider.
assessMonitor: Extent of crepitus, airway/voice changes, oxygenation, chest tube function.
interventions: Maintain tube patency/secure connections and prepare for further evaluation.
medicationSafety: No medication substitutes for correcting the mechanical cause.
teaching: Report new swelling or crackling sensation.
delegationScope: Finding must be promptly reported for licensed assessment.
examTrap: Massaging the crepitus away instead of evaluating the air leak.
oneLinePearl: Crepitus is a clue to escaping air, not a skin problem.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube complication guidance

title: After Chest-Tube Removal: Watch for Recurrent Pneumothorax
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After chest-tube removal, new dyspnea, hypoxemia, asymmetric breath sounds, expanding subcutaneous emphysema, or chest pain requires prompt evaluation for recurrent pneumothorax or other complication.
recognize: Sudden respiratory change after removal is not expected recovery.
priorities: Reassess respiratory status and dressing; escalate new deterioration immediately.
assessMonitor: Vital signs, oxygenation, breath sounds, chest symmetry, removal-site dressing.
interventions: Maintain occlusive dressing as ordered and prepare for imaging/reintervention if symptoms develop.
medicationSafety: Pain medicine can support breathing but should not mask worsening respiratory signs.
teaching: Report sudden shortness of breath or chest pain promptly after removal.
delegationScope: Post-removal respiratory reassessment is a licensed nursing responsibility.
examTrap: Assuming dyspnea is anxiety because the tube is already out.
oneLinePearl: Chest tube out does not end pneumothorax surveillance.

title: Pleural Infection Drainage: Cloudy Output Plus Fever Can Mean Empyema
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A pleural drain placed for infected fluid requires close monitoring for persistent sepsis, blocked drainage, and worsening respiratory status. Cloudy/purulent output, fever, and poor drainage need review.
recognize: Purulent drainage, fever, pleuritic pain, reduced output despite persistent symptoms.
priorities: Assess sepsis/respiratory cues and drainage-system patency; escalate deterioration.
assessMonitor: Temperature, respiratory status, drainage character/amount, insertion site, ordered labs.
interventions: Maintain aseptic handling and ordered drainage/suction plan.
medicationSafety: Administer antibiotics as ordered; do not delay cultures/clinical review when sepsis is suspected.
redFlags: Abrupt drainage cessation with worsening symptoms
teaching: Explain why fever and drainage changes need prompt reporting.
delegationScope: Output measurement may be delegated; infection interpretation/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Treating cloudy drainage as a normal color change without assessing infection.
oneLinePearl: Pleural drain plus fever = think source control and sepsis risk.

title: Chest-Tube Pain Control: Enough Relief to Breathe and Move
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Uncontrolled chest-tube pain can cause shallow breathing, poor cough, and immobility, but oversedation can worsen ventilation. Reassess both pain relief and respiratory function after treatment.
recognize: Splinting, shallow respirations, weak cough, reluctance to move, sedation after analgesia.
priorities: Use ordered multimodal pain relief and support cough/deep breathing/mobility while monitoring sedation.
assessMonitor: Pain score/behavior, respiratory rate/effort, oxygenation, sedation level, mobility.
interventions: Positioning, splinting, pulmonary hygiene, and timely analgesia as ordered.
medicationSafety: Opioids require sedation/respiratory monitoring and individualized dosing.
teaching: Pain control should help the patient breathe and move, not make them too sleepy to do so.
delegationScope: Pain reassessment and respiratory evaluation after analgesia require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Avoiding analgesia entirely because opioids can depress respirations.
oneLinePearl: Treat enough pain to ventilate—then reassess both comfort and breathing.
sourceBasis: NCBI Bookshelf chest tube nursing-management principles
